subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes; they fear God and keep out of debt as much as they can, and there may be some connection between the two. There is a lesson to be learned in western Canada from the attitude of the farmers of the East towards debt. I can recall my own youthful days, which is some time ago, when we looked upon debt as something to be utterly abhorred and avoided to the last. We thought that only in dire extremity, when one was in the last ditch, was it at at all excusable to get into debt, and then only as moderately as possible. Instead of amortizing debt from now to eternity we always tried to keep out of it. And that is
the reason why debt is not crucifying the people in the Maritime provinces. It is true that they are having tight times in some respects, but at least half of the people there are free from debt, and very few of the other half are overwhelmed with obligations, the simple reason being that they have never got into debt; they have played safe. Instead of running to the bank every now and then or hunting up the mortgage company and quarrelling with them because they would not give more, these people went to mother earth, dug the soil, improved the quality of their live stock and dairy products and thus obtained greater revenue from that source. And, withal, they kept their heads. Sometimes we in the West look down on the people of the East and call them stick-in-the-muds, slow and effete. I think, however, that we might to advantage acquire some degree of their caution, at least so far as the matter of debt is concerned. I have often wondered, if we struck the balance between the advantages and the disadvantages of mortgages as a means of developing agriculture, where the the difference would lie. I do not know. However, let us proceed with a consideration of agricultural conditions throughout the country, first in the Maritime provinces.
There is specialized farming in Prince Edward Island, at least to some extent; there is the raising of foxes in addition to specialization in certified seed potatoes, both of them very profitable industries. In New Brunswick there is a considerable area represented I understand by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Caldwell), that specializes in commercial potatoes. They have special equipment; their land is in shape; and their efforts during the war years were well rewarded. Now, however, the war is over and they are faced with a tremendous tariff in the United States, so that the potato growers in that part of the Dominion are in hard circumstances. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is always the way; the man who engages in specialized farming of any kind, even dairying, will sooner or later find the same thing befalls his industry. Possibly dairying and. hog-growing which go together, constitute the safest line; there is the least amount of disease associated with them and the least liability to collapse. But specialized farming, whether it be potato growing in New Brunswick, fruit growing in the beautiful Niagara peninsula, or in the Annapolis valley, or specialized fruit growing in British Columbia, all run infinitely more risks than are encountered in diversified farming. That doctrine is as old as the hills, and yet a great

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
many of us are so slow to appreciate it. I suppose we can be excused for reluctantly admitting it. Anyone who ever got the imperial feeling that comes to a man on a threshing machine, who sees the stream of golden grain running into the waggon box, and afterwards takes it to the elevator and gets his cheque, will agree that it is no wonder that people specialize. There is a sufficient modicum of the gambling instinct in most of us to succumb to such a temptation. I have never been a gold miner myself but I can imagine a man digging and prospecting for twenty years in the hope of turning up something, until he is finally bankrupt. But we must play a safe game in agriculture. If we do, we shall be able to obtain a living and build ourselves comfortable homes and provide something for old age.	Let
every man do this, so that he may be his own household king, beholden to no man. And that is what is really worth while. So much for the Maritime provinces. I regret that I cannot spend more time dealing with their conditions. They form an interesting part of the country and this summer I hope to make another itinerary and have it carried out. Then I shall be able to speak at first hand.
I had an opportunity of visiting the experimental farms in Quebec last year, and some of my friends described my references thereto as a travelogue. I suppose I know in a vague way what that is, but I had an interesting time, whether you call it a travelogue or any kind of "logue". Agriculture in Quebec presents an interesting study. I do not think any province has made the same development in agriculture during the last twenty years. It may be said that Quebec has had further to go, that its agriculture was primitive twenty years ago, and therefore those responsible for the affairs of state had the opportunity of their lives. I am not ^oing to discuss that feature. All I know is that in co-operative dairying I am safe in saying that no other province has made the same progress during the last ten years, in fact in co-operative marketing generally. Our estimates were scarcely through the House where some doubting Thomases were wondering whether anyone would take advantage of the cold storage subsidies, when we had two applications from co-operative societies in the neighbourhood of Montreal and Quebec cities-not the Harbour Cold Storage concern that I referred to the other day, but real co-operative societies run by farmers. They have been asked if they will be able to comply with our conditions and so earn these subsidies. Co-operation is

the spirit of the age. I am not one of those who think that middlemen are a bunch of grafters or parasites; not at all. I think a certain class of middlemen are necessary, otherwise we must give the same service ourselves. During the present hard times we have been compelled in many places to adopt co-operation and dispense with some of the services of the middlemen in order that business may be conducted at a profit. But, remember, we are merely doing the service that in former years had been relegated by custom to middlemen.
A good part of eastern Quebec has a climate not exactly like that of the Canadian West, but sufficiently similar to make it difficult to grow fodder corn. The result is that few silos have been constructed. A considerable portion of that interesting province has been denuded of its trees, and farmers are endeavouring to till a reluctant soil that will scarcely grow a crop. It is in such sections of Quebec that you find hard times. We had a man before the Agricultural committee from Ste. Anne's. There are some beautiful spots around there, and also some very hard-looking sections which should never have been brought under cultivation. That witness told us a rueful story, as if the conditions in his locality were representative of those obtaining throughout his province. The substance of his lamentations was this:	I am on poor land and I cannot
borrow any money. He wanted what are known as additional credit facilities. I asked him if he had not sufficient credit facilities from mortgage companies and the like. He replied that these companies would not lend him any money or only very little. Upon further inquiry I found he was actually, trying to eke out an existence on land that should have been left as forest. But there is a certain amount of intermediate quality land between these splendid valleys and the absolutely poor land where the farmers get along pretty well. But if they knew they could grow first-class ensilage by cultivating sunflowers-something which will flourish in a much colder climate than Quebec-their profits would be increased to a very great extent. Such ensilage can be kept over from year to year for provision against drouth. It is not necessary to build an upright silo. If a farmer is too poor to undertake such an outlay he can build a silo in the ground. A hundred years ago or more we find that in the north of Ireland and other parts of Europe the farmers put ensilage in a hole in the ground-sometimes brewers' grain, anything in fact that they wanted to keep in a semi-acid condition. So a man does not need to have much capital to construct a silo for his dairy stock. The use of a silo will encourage him to go into a much

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
more profitable form of dairying. In other words, to be profitable to the maximum dairying should be all the year around, not merely during the summer. I can recall my own boyhood days, when we stopped milking the cows and the milk factories closed we used to think it a day of rejoicing, for to lads of fourteen years of age the work was laborious and the hours very long. Well, the moment that the cows went on winter rations so many farmers put them through on such low maintenance rations that in the spring they were skin poor. That is not right. Those are the conditions under which dairying largely failed in Ontario years ago. Naturally there is a tendency if you are not getting anything from the cow to feed her very sparingly. Of course, this is a great mistake.
I hardly know what to say about agriculture in Ontario. You will travel over many seas and in many lands, Mr. Speaker, before you will find a better country than old Ontario. I do not think it necessary to spend very much time in describing farming conditions in Ontario.	As to suggesting improved methods, I would hesitate long before venturing to do so. Possibly one reason why they have not very many experimental farms in Ontario is that they do not need them. But even in Ontario I venture to say the farmers are only waking up to two or three things that we should have been alive to twenty or thirty years ago. Of course, we all think of living when we should be thinking of dying. In the western Ontario peninsula there has been a tremendous hazard in the growing of fruit. The government that preceded us, in one of its moments of enterprise and progress, built a pre-cooling plant at Grimsby. That has proved to be a wonderful transforming institution in the fruit district of the Niagara peninsula. If they could get one or two more such institutions it would simply revolutionize fruit-growing by enabling them to pick their fruit from the tree and rush it into cold storage. Last year that institution was kept open day and night for weeks to the great advantage of the local fruit growers.
We are falling behind in our dairy exports. Reports from the Motherland indicate that our competitors in the Antipodes are getting away ahead of us. They have adopted modern methods in the manufacture of their butter and cheese; we have not; that is all there is to it. It does not follow that we are inferior or incompetent in these matters, because it was a Canadian in the person of Mr. Ruddick, our present dairy commissioner, who organized the New Zealand dairy industry. There is a
Canadian to-day in charge down there. Well, if a Canadian can do it in New Zealand, why cannot a Canadian do it here? They have many disadvantages, on the other hand they have many advantages too. Two of our representatives have just returned from a visit to New Zealand and Australia. I havp not yet received their reports, but I have had a preliminary report from Mr. Ruddick. He has also given certain statements to the press and certain evidence before the Agricultural committee with respect to our dairying requirements. In effect he says that if we are to keep pace with our brothers in the Antipodes we must modernize our methods. We have antiquated cheese factories in this country. They are too small to give a proper turnover, to give a profit either to the farmer or to the maker of cheese; too small to enable the turning out of a large volume of uniform quality. The cheese is graded too soon, taken out of the factory too soon, not cooled properly, not ripened properly; and the result is that it cannot compete with the first-class article that is put on the market of Great Britain by our competitors. We shall have to speed up if we are to avoid falling further back. For twenty-five years we were the topnotchers on the British market in the matter of cheese. We are second now, and unless we watch out we shall soon be third. We never were first in butter that I know of; we were, I think, third for a time. I do not know where we are now; I do not know where we shall be three years from now if we do not take warning and get our dairying on a better basis. That is all I will venture to say at this time until I get the report of the commissioners who journeyed to New Zealand and saw what was the last word in this connection. Well, I do not know that it is, in fact, the last word; it is like the tariff-there is no finality; even death is not final. And there is no finality about dairying. But the investigations being made have to do with the last word in dairying so far as its application to Canada is concerned. I hope, therefore, that I shall have the sympathy and support of the dairymen of eastern Canada, who have been exceedingly tolerant of a western man who is not supposed to know anything about dairying. I hope we shall have their co-operation in putting the dairying of Ontario and Quebec on a better basis so that we may be where we ought to be so far as the British market is concerned, at the top of the list-where we were before, where we should be again and may be again if we only will. But I want to warn you that you will have to submit to even more restrictions than

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
you do submit to now. There was a great howdy-do when Hon. Manning Doherty introduced last spring for the first time the policy of buying milk on the basis of quality and butter fat content. Just think of it: after fifty years only now waking up to the necessity of paying according to the quality of the goods you get. Why, you might as well make a flat rate for horses as have a flat rate for milk. The same may be said in regard to the cream, because in all these things we have fallen behind. Mr. Doherty is to be congratulated for taking the initiative in this matter, because as a rule the man who breaks the ice in this direction in an old province is going to get rapped oyer the knuckles for it. Mr. Doherty was sufficiently near this election to make it a little dangerous for him; I was sufficiently far from the election to make it comparatively safe for me to introduce this principle of grading. People would come into my office and tell me what was going to happen to me if they were not permitted to carry on their dairy boards as they had been carried on for the last forty years and to make cheese and grade it just as they pleased. Well, nothing happened; there has been no upheaval. .The new grading system came into effect on the first of April and on succeeding days we woke up and found things just about as they were, except that our butter and cheese were going over with the government grade stamped on each package.
Mr.. WARNER: May I ask the hon. gentleman which province took the most prizes in last year's butter market?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think it was the province of Alberta. I am just coming to the breezy West now; I cannot afford to spend any more time on Ontario. Now we have to go through that great area of rocks and mountains and plains west of the lakes-[DOT] and I will deal with the three prairies as one country. They are to a large extent the same so far as this subject is concerned, though it is true that in some other respects they are quite different. In the matter of dairying Alberta takes the lead both as to quantity and as to quality and prizes. Of course it is an easy matter for a man who is an adept at it, and who specializes in assembling cream from the best patrons, to make a high quality of butter. The western provinces have come to the front, but not because the dairymen there are better than those in the East; they are not; they are far more primitive dairymen than the eastern dairymen are. They have more primitive surroundings; they have poorer live stock; they have not as good barns; they have not had as much experience

as the eastern man, having been at it a shorter time. Yet, because they have adopted proper methods, their butter commands five shillings a hundred more than any eastern butter that goes on the British market. I am sure my eastern friends will not object to our saying that; we have not much to boast of there, you know, outside of our wheat. I tell you that our country out there, notwithstanding the long winter, can be profitably turned to dairying. The adoption of new and improved methods, the paying for milk and cream on the basis of quality, enables the butter makers to turn out a first-class article. The chain of cold storages that has been established in that country enables us to take care of the butter until such time as we wish to ship it to the Old Land. Some hon. gentlemen have spoken disparagingly of co-operative activities, but it was the co-operative creameries of Regina that sold and shipped overseas more than sixty carloads of high-class butter last year-the record shipment from Canada to the markets of Great Britain.
There is not so much disparagement of diversified farming by our Progressive friends this year, and I will give them credit for it. There was last year; they are learning, like the rest of us. There was a good deal of tee-heeing and poking of fun at dairying and diversified farming. Some of our friends across the way are good at telling humourous stories. There was one very funny one that we all laughed at; it was the experience of the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. McConica), whom we are glad to see in his seat again, in connection with sheep growing;
I am sure you will all recall it. Our western country has up to quite recently been a purely grain growing country except in some parts of Manitoba, where they have been diversifying for many years; we have been specializing in the growing of grain. There have been men who have grown wealthy in that business. The fact is that you either grow wealthy fairly quickly or you go broke even more quickly-one of the two. If you are a good manager; if you are young and healthy and vigorous and can get up betimes in the morning and will go to bed while you can; if you have the capacity of getting work out of men; if either you or some of your boys know how to run a gasoline engine or some other kind of power machine to supplement your farm labour at times, and if you are a regular nigger driver, why, you can hold the pace for ten or fifteen years and you may become independently wealthy. Some have done it in less than that. But that is a pretty hard life, Mr. Speaker; it is no wonder some of those

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
who follow it have to go to California or British Columbia. I know of one gentleman whose case just comes to my mind now. I know his experience from the year one so far as the West is concerned. He was in my employ at a dollar a day for a week, and at the end of the week I got to my last dollar and had to dismiss him. But that is how he started out; and to-day he is worth I do not know how much. I know he has $30,000 worth of Canadian bonds; I know he has a good many Canadian Pacific Railway stocks; in fact, he is in the plutocratic class now. He also has shares in one of the local banks. And he did not make it all by working his family day and night, either, because he has not got any family. His name is Elmer Shaw, if anyone wants to look the gentleman up.	_
We have had a series of varying experiences in agriculture in western Canada; it has been a case of make or break. When that country was settled first there was a great *rush of immigrants. That was the case in the early days of the construction of the Canadian Pacific, at the time I went there myself, .and it occurred also later on, in the early days of the present century, when people were coming from all quarters of the globe to take up land in this El Dorado. Naturally a great many people came in who proved to be misfits; the attraction of a homestead for $10 was very great indeed. The thirst for land is strong in the breast of the average individual, and we still have land to gratify that thirst, but in the coming of people from all quarters of the globe, from all climes and all directions, including the republic to the south and eastern Canada, you are bound to have men who have failed in other countries and are desirous of trying their luck once more on this new land and having a farm for ten dollars. Unfortunately the same methods they puisued which caused their failure elsewhere would be very apt to occasion their failure in the West also.
I am not one of those who disparage inexperienced settlers. I know men who went out there who did not know anything about agriculture except that they knew that they	did not	know anything	about
it-and believe me that is the start; when you know that you do not know anything about agriculture, then you are ready to learn at the feet of anybody whom you think does know, but if you go there thinking you know it all the chances are that you will meet with disaster before you learn the peculiar requirements of prairie agriculture. A number of these people have hung on. I know a number of them who through all 176

these years have been just one lap ahead of the sheriff. In times like these when money is tight, and these facilities we are talking about for borrowing money are not multiplied by two, these people are squeezed pretty hard. They borrowed all the money they could get and went into one hole to get out of the previous one. Instead of improving their methods they wanted to improve their opportunities for borrowing, and then they quarrelled with the mortgage company because they could not get still more.	*
We will have to assume a different attitude towards debt, Mr. Speaker, before we get our stride properly on the prairies again. I can recall the time especially during and before the war, when some of us took a certain amount of pride in actually boasting about borrowing every dollar we could get on our land, and then going abroad and spending it like a lord, investing it in this and that possibly not connected with the farm and then expecting the farm to carry that obligation and help wipe it out. That is not fair. Very few debts contracted in the West have been spent on agriculture, and I say that advisedly.
I think I am safe in saying that three out of four first mortgages are for the purpose of consolidating store bills and dead horses and such like, with not one dollar invested in any productive enterprise that will help pay back the loan. That was the condition. We rushed in there pell-mell, enthused with the possibilities of the development of that country We thought the thing would never end. We sowed to the wind and are to-day reaping the whirlwind. This condition of affairs, aggravated by the war, has occasioned many, many tragedies on the prairies. There is no question about it. It is something that would make your heart bleed, Mr. Speaker. But what are you going to do about it? Men who lend money must have security.
I have in mind another instance, and there is nothing that could be morp tragic than what I am going to describe. Both of these parties were labourers of my own at the time they were married. They started out for themselves with nothing but the prospect of getting a . home for themselves and $45, and that was not in cash. They had a three-year old filly, and they got a chattel mortgage on the filly for $45, more than what they paid for it, and made the first payment on a quarter section of Canadian Pacific Railway land. They added to that by one means and another till they had five quarter sections, all on time except the initial payment. They bought machinery on time, and horses on time.
The Budget-Mr. Motherwell

I will not tell you how they got them or stood off their creditors, I do not know; I could not do it and succeed. After twenty-four years of that kind of experience, growing magnificent crops, if you like, and raising a family of twelve, they are finally crowded out on to the street by the mortgage company. If you did not know the history of that, Mr. Speaker, you would think it was something terrible. It is something terrible if you do not know the circumstances. But under the circumstances nothing else could befall them. The only wonder is that it did not happen long ago. There is no country in the world except the Canadian West which would have stood such abuse of farm and credit, and where this couple could have lasted for twenty-four years. I might say that the neighbours helped that couple for years and are helping them yet. Some friends in Alberta wrote to the First Minister, and the First Minister passed the letter over to me. It is a great place down here to pass the buck, you know, Mr. Speaker. I got a letter describing the case, and I told the First Minister that there was nothing else for it. I knew the couple exceedingly well. Some of the boys and girls were capable of working out, and I advised them to work for their neighbours. Hundreds of men who would make first-class labourers, are only fourth, or fifth-class managers for themselves. It takes a long time to find it out. My advice to such would be to let the shoemaker stick to his last, let the man perform that service he is best fitted for. If he cannot make a living managing his own affairs, if he is a faithful labourer and gives proper service, he may soon find himself in better circumstances than his employer.

Does the minister mention that type as representative of the farmers of the West?
Mr. MOTHERWEI.L: Which one? I have tried to describe two, the two extremes-the (man who was a bounder and was turned oa the street after twenty-four years, and the man who was a good manager, a mechanic, who knew how to get labour out of his men, got up betimes in the morning, took care of his business and became wealthy. It just shows, Mr. Speaker, how much depends on the individual. It has been said, though this is extreme, of course, that some men would make a living in the Sahara desert while others would starve in the Garden of Eden.
Does the minister mean to represent the man who did not go into debt as being prosperous to-day?

Debt is a good thing sometimes. It is like fire. Fire is good as long as you are the boss, but when fire becomes your boss, then look out. Debt is a good thing, I suppose, as long as you are master. It is a good servant but a mighty bad master. If we have to go into debt let us go into it just as little as possible, and just to the extent that we think we can get out of it in reasonable time.
I am afraid the minister did not catch my point. Does he mean to say that agriculture in the West to-day, in the case of the men who keep clear of debt, is prospering?

I say that the men who keRt out of debt or went into debt only very moderately are in safe circumstances to-day, and there are less failures among these than among any other class of people. I say that advisedly.
Are they prosperous to-day?

Yes, they are prosperous to-day. The fact that they are out of debt is a good indication of that. I sav further, I would like to sound a note of warning right now. I do not think the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) exactly voiced my sentiments.

I would like to ask the minister how he reconciles his statement about farmers keeping out of debt with the statement that was made in the Agricultural committee that for all the municipalities of Saskatchewan this year the records show an average unpaid tax of $37 per quarter section.

If my hon. friend will wait for a minute or two until I get to that point I will be very glad to deal with it; it is the very next item on my notes. I would like to sound a note of warning with respect to this amortization of debt, this funding of debt. One of the reasons why the man with little debt, or only sufficient debt to be controllable, is better off than the man with a big burden and heavy interest charges is this: All the time he has the consciousness of being a landed proprietor; he is sitting under his own fig tree, the dwelling he occupies is his own, and even if he has a little debt that home is not endangered. Therefore I say that the man in that condition is better off

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
than the man who is so burdened down with debt' he does not know whether his home belongs to him or whether the mortgage company owns it-there is no question about that. And the idea of asking a man to undertake an amortization of debt which is to run for thirty years 1 Why, if he is thirty years old he will be a man of my age before he knows the sweet joy of being the sole proprietor of that land. I say that is paralyzing to his efforts to make a success of that farm, yet it is exactly one of the mistakes we are making. Instead of pleading before our committees for more facilities to borrow money we should turn our attention to digging wealth out of the soil and buying better live stock.
Now I will deal with the question asked by my hon. friend the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould).

Seeing that the hon. member is about to take up a new branch of the subject we had better call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
I had forgotten exactly what it was.

I made refer ence to evidence given before the Agricultural committee, that there was an average tax debt this year of $37 per quarter section on every quarter section in Saskatchewan, a debt that was recorded on municipal lands.

Does that mean bonded indebtedness?
Mr. GOULD- No, average tax.

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
Mr. MOTHERWELL- I have a bigger tax than that on my land.
Mr. GOULD- This is an unpaid tax on
each quarter section.

I do not doubt that either. If my hon. friend is familiar-and I am sure he is-with collecting municipal taxes, he knows that if things are bad, it is not the municipality or the government that is paid first. I do not think my hon. friend wants to make a case against any party. He wants to get at the facts as I do, and I want to get between these two extremes that we have heard of during the session.

I was trying to establish the point that people who own land will not permit arrears of $37 per quarter section of land on an average throughout the whole province, if agricultural conditions warrant their paying it.

I do not know if that is correct. Possibly evidence of that nature was given before the Agricultural committee; but I am going to read to the House a statement made in the budget debate in the Saskatchewan assembly by the premier of that province. I think we can take the premier of that province as a reliable authority. I must confess that since leaving provincial politics, I have not kept close tab on municipal debts. There are some municipalities that have no bonded debt at all; I happen to be fortunate enough to live in one myself. That municipality has never had any bonded debt unless perhaps it has incurred one within the last two years, for during that time I have not been there to know. If, however, the same reeve is in office who has been there for many years, then I venture to say there is no such debt yet. But with regard to the rest of the bonded debt, $40 or $37, on current taxes overdue, the situation is getting better every day in every way. I have a communication here from the Minister of Agriculture of Saskatchewan, Hon. Mr. Hamilton, to this effect:
Replying to your wire of the 14th instant, I am enclosing herewith .typed copy of Premier Dunning's budget speech. The printed copies have not yet come to hand.
This is the letter accompanying the budget speech which he forwarded to me, but he gives certain information personally in addition.
In October last a campaign was inaugurated for ,he selling of Saskatchewan bonds for the Farm Loans Board, and to date an amount of $902,300 has been received. Of this amount $300,000 was subscribed iby the Hail Commission, and the rest practically all by farmers.

I have no records for the other provinces, but I think that Manitoba's situation is somewhat better than the condition in Saskatchewan municipally, while the situation in Alberta may possibly be somewhat worse. As I say however, I have not the facts before me, and that is merely my assumption. It will be noted that over $900,000 worth of Saskatchewan bonds were sold last year so that the Farm Loans Board might have these funds from the farmers and be able to re-loan the money to less fortunate farmers. That is their scheme. Out of that $900,000, $300,000 worth was purchased by the Hail Insurance Commission. Where did that commission get the money? They got it through the premiums from the farmers; they had that much to the good this year and invested it in Saskatchewan farm loan bonds. This is the information that comes to me from the Hon. Mr. Hamilton. He then refers me to page 27 of the budget speech of Premier Dunning wherein he says will be found reference to the sale of Saskatchewan debentures. I will not go into that phase of the situation. I do not know whether the information given me is correct, but I do know Mr. Hamilton to be a responsible man. Of course, it will be a difficult matter to get at the real facts in regard to the average overdue taxes in the municipalities of Saskatchewan, for the reason that the returns are not all in. However, I will accept my hon. friend's statement as to the amount on the average that is overdue. Again, I do not know that this statement is correct, but I will accept it any way for the purposes of this debate. Now let me turn to Premier Dunning's statement, which is rather voluminous. He said in part:
It is not possible to say truthfully on this occasion that our economic problems are solved, that we are a very prosperous people or a very prosperous province. But I think the conclusion the House will reach, after hearing the information which I have to present on this occasion, will be that at least we have passed the low point; and, to use the phrase that is often used, we have scraped bottom and are now on the improvement so far as economic conditions of our people are concerned and the financial position of the province and its municipalities.
I am sure that this must be regarded as pleasant information. Mr. Dunning states, "We have touched bottom, we have turned the comer, we are going to be able we hope, with the experience of the past before us, to make the grade."
Glad to hear it.
Oh, oh.

I do not know
whether my hon. friends are rejoicing at the possibility of their being able to put a differ-

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
ent construction on the phrase I have used, "touching bottom," from the meaning that Premier Dunning intends it to convey. I do not know whether it is the bottomless pit that hon. gentlemen have in mind, but apparently the worse construction is the one they entertain. Would it not be better to take that better meaning, "Whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report," and so on? I think it would be better for hon. gentlemen to take that more favourable construction when referring to their own country; I do not see what pleasure they can take in fouling their own nests.
What we want is the truth.

If hon. gentlemen
can take any fun out of this I am loath to deny them the pleasure. All I desire to do is to give the information to the House. Let me continue the quotation:
This probably is largely due to the way in which Nature or Providence treated us in 1922 as compared with the previous year.
Surely Providence plays a part in our harvests and in our lives.
It is also due to the fact that our people during 1921 learned the stern hard lesson of the necessity for economy and thrift in all their dealings and work.
Premier Dunning attributes the good result to economy and thrift plus a good crop, which enabled them to turn the corner. The people learnt the lesson that was taught by the perfect orgy of extravagance in connection with borrowing which had been indulged in. Most of us have been guilty of such extravagance, Mr. Speaker. I confess that I too have been bitten by the bug of extravagance. Some of us, however, kept our businesses very reasonably in hand and when the fatal day of deflation came we were able to recover our balance without disaster, while others went with such impetus that they toppled over the precipice, with the result that everything is gone except the howl.
Our wheat acreage in 1922 decreased as compared with 1921 by over one million acres, but in spite of that the yield of wheat increased from 14.8 per acre to 20.25, or giving total figures from 201,000,000 bushels to 251,000,000 bushels in 1922, an increased production of over 50,000,000 bushels of wheat.
The province that can produce 250,000,000 bushels of the best wheat in the world surely should not feel too hard up. Surely some of it must accrue to the people after it has passed through the various avenues to the markets of the world.

Would the minister give it as his opinion that the men who grew this
wheat were able to sell it for more than cost of production?

The last time I
operated my farm was in the year 1921, and if I had attended to it myself instead of gallivanting around the country preparing for the election of that year I would have made it pay. As it was I did dot make it pay, because I was not there to superintend and manage the farm myself; and I do not think that any man can make a farm pay unless he stays on the job. Now, to come to the matter of price.
The average net price to the farmer for the 1922 crop will be 85 cents per bushel, or 10 cents per bushel more than 1921.
That was the estimate made more than three months ago, in the month of March. The price has gone up 10 or 15 cents a bushel; at least that 85 cents will have increased to 90 cents by the time the figures are all in. So much for the statement of Premier Dunning. Now, there is not much money in exclusive wheat growing; there is no question about that; neither would there be much money in any business in which the by-products were not utilized. How much money would there be in any industry in Canada if the byproducts were dissipated in the way they are on many wheat farms on which there is no live stock?

Before the minister leaves
Premier Dunning's statement would he mind reading the premier's expression of opinion in regard to that late budget just brought down?
Yes, I think I can give it to my hon. friend. I have not got it here.
Oh, oh.

Yes, I will give it to my hon. friend. I wired Premier Dunning this morning and I will give my hon. friend to-morrow a copy of my telegram. The concluding paragraph of Mr. Dunning's speech is something like this- by the way, would my hon. friend read Henry Wise Wood's expression of opinion on the budget?
Oh, oh.

I have to apologize to my hon. friend the Premier of Saskatchewan. I do not want to make such invidious comparisons of that nature. The last paragraph of Premier Dunning's speech was something like this:
We might take this budget and that of last year as moderate indications of a desire on the part of the

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
government to carry out their tariff pledges of 1919. But no western Liberal will take the ground that these should be the final word in the redemption of the tariff pledges given at the national convention of 1919.
No stability.
That was the substance of his speech, and I can say yes to that. And who said it was the last word?
The Minister of Finance.

Nobody said it was the last word. I was very sorry to hear the terms mentioned by the hon. leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke). I am sure he did not mean that "finality" and "stability" were synonymous terms; and yet one might infer as much from the way in which he used them in his address yesterday. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) said distinctly there was no finality, that what parliament did today it might undo to-morrow. I think the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) gave a very apt illustration of it. We have had stability during the last two years, but not necessarily finality. I do not think we can have finality in anything.
What is the hon. gentleman's definition of stability?
I cannot improve on the definition given by the hon. member for Brantford.

That was political
agility.

My hon. friend
can supply his own interpretation.
Does the hon. minister mean by stability that we have been on the bottom for the last two years that he referred to a little while ago?

No, I decline to constitute myself the interpretation clause of the act. I want to produce some further evidence, Mr. Speaker, of the condition of agriculture-not from myself at all for I have not been an active farmer during the last two years except very casually. Learning something from the press of what we might expect this session, we sent out last January a questionnaire, prepared by my deputy and myself, to some hundred correspondents throughout the three prairie provinces. It is too voluminous to deal with in detail; I am only going to take the two last questions which are really the essential ones. The first is:
Is mixed farming, that is, raising beef cattle, dairying, pork production and poultry keeping, making any progress in your district ?

The other question is:
Have you any suggestions to offer as to .the best line for farmers to follow in your district in order to make a greater success of their operations?
A great many of these correspondents are practical farmers; some of them are operators at illustration stations and have a little advantage in that way because they are probably in advance of the average farmer in experimentation and keeping their eyes on the results therefrom. I have summarized the answers under three colums, headed Yes, Some and No.
The first question, as to whether they are going into mixed farming or not, is I believe the most important, because after all that is the solution of many of the difficulties of our western farmers. From the province of Manitoba every answer to that question is yes. So they are on the right track to improve their condition. Answers were received from the city of Winnipeg, Brandon, central Manitoba, Treesbamk, Morden, Fort Garry, Dauphin, Lake Winnipeg to Manitoba, Manitoba (Live Stock Branch) and Arthur.
From the province of Saskatchewan sixty-five per cent of the answers were to the effect that the writers were going gradually into mixed farming. These answers were received from Meota, Scott, Saskatoon and Prince Albert, Ogema, Lloydminster, S. E. Saskatchewan, Tugaska, Avonlea, Indian Head-I have often said that when Indian Head started to go into mixed farming nearly every other place would be thinking of following its example, because that is one of the earliest successful wheat areas of Saskatchewan-Regina, Moose Jaw, Prince Albert and Radville. Six say they are going some into it, namely, North Portal, Riverhurst, Saskatoon, Davidson and Pambrun. Forty-one per cent say no, they are not going into mixed farming. I hope they are mistaken in their answers. These negative replies came from Wood Mountain, Kindersley and Qu'Appelle. I do not quite understand what part of Qu'Appelle unless it is the village in the valley, for it cannot be Qu'Appelle Station, this having always been a diversified district.
From Alberta we received replies that the tendency is to go into mixed farming. These answers came from the following districts: North Alberta, Edmonton, Lacombe, Lacombe (Reed), Calgary District, Alberta, Alberta and Peace River, Grassy Lake, Pincher Creek, Oka-toks, Calgary (Bain), Red Deer, and Alberta (Cormie).
Nine districts say they are going into mixed farming some, and four districts answer in the

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
negative. These latter are Wainwright-by the way, from what I saw when I was there last year it would appear that they were not going into mixed farming. The fact that the great buffalo herd, of which my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior has charge, is stationed at Wainwright would go to show that it is an excellent live stock country.
Does the minister imply that Wainwright is not a mixed farming country?
I should think it was to some extent.
It certainly is.
But the report here says that they are not going much into mixed farming.
The report is wrong.

In answer to the other question. Have you any suggestions as to the best line for farmers to follow in your district in order to make a greater success of their operations? We heard from Manitoba pretty much to the same effect as in reply to the first question; 95 per cent advocate mixed and diversified farming. Here are some of the individual answers. One says:
Cattle-better sires and better market conditions- dairying-increase live stock, more alfalfa, sunflowers, fodder corn etc., hogs, poultry, smaller farms and winter feeding of beef cattle, cut down expenses and work more.
I do not suppose any one in this House is in need of that advice-each works hard when on the farm. In the case of Saskatchewan 95 per cent of the correspondents give the same advice:
Dairying and hog raising-better business methods- smaller farms-more corn-smaller farms, worked better.
These are all good suggestions. They also write:
Cut down costs-too far from the railway to farm-more summer fallow-improved market conditions- farm better

keep better cows, etc -
Now here is one answer, Mr. Speaker, that is rather unusual. This correspondent says: "Pray for rain." Now, this may be more effective and less expensive than introducing a second Hatfield the rainmaker. I commend it to the attention of my hon. friends. Then, in Albenta, "mixed farming," "better live stock"-you would think it was the same man who wrote all of this. These questions come from all over the country, and surely what everybody says in this respect must have some element of truth in it. "Dual purpose cattle; better quality of poultry." A number of them stress the necessity for improved live
stock. It seems to me that no one is doing his best on a farm who insists on Keeping scrub beef cattle, low-grade cows, razorback hogs, and dunghill hens. There is no virtue in live stock unless it will more than pay for the cost of keeping it. I do not think, however, that it is necessary to develop this phase of the question. Here is a practically unanimous verdict as to how we may better ourselves as a result of the effort of the individual. Later in my remarks I will come to some of the larger public questions and refer to the manner in which the individual can be helped in some measure by the state. But now I am dealing with those phases of agriculture in which the man himself is largely the dominant factor. There is no doubt that in 30 or 85 per cent of the cases the success of the man on the land depends upon his own individuality.
A gentleman whose name I have forgotten was passing through Ottawa in January, and we were discussing these things. He estimated that the farmers had 100,000,000 bushels of grain in their possession or in transit or at the terminals at that time, subject to no obligation. I thought the estimate was pretty high and I wired Mr. Snow of the Grain Commission, who replied that on the last of January there were 75,000,000 bushels of unsold wheat, with obligations attached to some of it that was at Fort William. However, over half of it was in the farmers' granary with no obligations against it. I do not think many of the men who held wheat in their granaries until the first of February mortgaged it, although I believe they can do so if they desire. My point is this: A country that can carry over from harvest time until the first of February 75,090,000 bushels of wheat, worth slightly over $1 a bushel, or $75,000,000, cannot be in a very bad condition. I have no doubt that this estimate of the Grain Commission is correct; as e matter of fact I think it is low. As I say, the obligations against this wheat were comparatively small. There would be, of course, whatever payment they would get in advance, whatever drafts might be attached to the bills of lading. And I may say that since the rapid deflation of wheat in 1920, considerably more care has been exercised in attaching drafts to bills of lading.
Would the minister not suggest that out of that 75,000,000 bushels, provision must be made for seed as well as for advances made on the grain?

No; allowance was made for that. It was the estimate made of what had to go forward.

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
Now, we have some figures with regard to other matters besides grain. We cannot live by grain alone or by growing it. There are too many plant diseases, too many insect pests. The way to develop insect pests is to grow the one kind of plant food for them all the time; if you do that you will soon be visited by some kind of fungus or destructive insect. That is the condition we are in now. The fungus pest is continuing its depredations; the wheat stem sawfly has become more prevalent. Then, there are the grasshoppers. We never heard of grasshoppers in Saskatchewan until a few years ago and they have been a terrible scourge.
I am going to deal now with cattle. We are developing rapidly as a stock growing country. I am sure the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) did not go headlong into wheat growing alone; he stood fast as a farmer; he carried on diversified agriculture and grew good live stock. During the calendar year 1922, 18,000 head of live stock were shipped to Great Britain, valued at over
82.000.	000. To the United States we shipped 217,000 head, valued at over $5,000,000 and to other countries 4,000 head valued at $391,000. Our total exports were 240,000, valued at $8,000,000.
I have here an estimate by the Dairy branch with respect to the total production of dairy products. Last year the total production of creamery butter in all Canada was
128.000.	000 pounds, of a total value of $48,000,000. Of cheese the total production was
162.000.	000 of a total value of $28,000,000. The total dairy production in Canada in 1921 [DOT]-milk, casein, milk powder, skim milk, sterilized milk, and so on-totalled $212,000,000. We know that in the eastern provinces dairying is largely carried on, and we are just beginning to realize the necessity of regarding dairying in the West as something more than a mere side line. In 1921, 8.000,000 pounds of creamery butter were produced in Manitoba; last year the production was 10,000,000 poimds, an increase of 2,000,000 pounds. In Saskatchewan in 1921, the production was
7.000.	000 pounds; in 1922, nearly 9,000,000 pounds. In Alberta in 1921 the production was 13,000,000 pounds and in 1922, 15,000,000 poimds. There is the hope of Alberta. I am sure the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) would, if he had the liberty that we all like to enjoy, tell us how he kept his head above water, how dairying kept him afloat as it has kept many another man, especially in the pioneer days when there was nothing else to live on but the cows.

I was going to give the total exports of wheat from Canada, but I do not think I need give the figures; they are familiar to all hon. members.

I understood that the minister when he was out West in a recent byelection promised that the Hudson Bay railway would be ready by Christmas. I am afraid it will be like getting the boys out of the trenches, and take a much longer time than that.

My hon. friend is
referring to the time when I was out West on that interesting Easter holiday. I may say that I did not hear anything about that report until I got back nearly to Ottawa. I saw it on the train in some of the morning papers-of course, we read everything on the train-and that was the first time I ever heard of it. I took particular care not to discuss the Hudson Bay railway very much in that by-election. I certainly never even suggested such a thing as the railway being ready by Christmas. What is more, if I had, the people in the Moose Jaw '-iding. especially, in that district interested in branch lines, certainly would not have been in favour of it because they would have figured out that the more, mileage built on the Hudson Bay railway the less money there would be for branch lines in the southern part of that riding. Whoever started that fake yarn did not know the situation in Moose Jaw. The people down there want branch lines, and they want them very badly. I may add that in spite of the result of that election I had occasion to make a recommendation regarding some of the earlier lines to be taken care of and one of them was in the southern part of Moose Jaw riding. I recommended that because the people need it, no matter whether they were foolish or not about whom they selected. There is nothing like casting bread upon the waters, Mr. Speaker.
I am going now to deal with an interesting subject.
Hear, hear.

I hope I am not too tiresome to my hon. friends. I try to be as little wearisome as possible but it is a big story, the story of agriculture in Canada.
We dealt with the subject of immigration in this House for five consecutive days, and I did not feel like rising and further obstructing the estimates of my colleague to my right (Mr. Stewart, ArgenteuiP I want to congratu-

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
late the leader of the Progressive party, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) for the sane and wise attitude that he has taken on the question of immigration, not only in this House but in Winnipeg and elsewhere in Manitoba where his voice was heard after he received the position he now occupies. He spoke on the subject at Brandon too, I believe, at the convention. He takes the ground that a great many of our difficulties would be solved if we had more people. He does not think it is wise to induce any more people to come to this country until those who are here are on Easy street. Well, if we wait till that time comes we will wait till the crack of doom, for a lot of people will never get on Easy street; they are not built that way. He takes the ground that the railway situation would also be solved by immigration. We have too much country and too few people. Twice as many people would not cost twice as much to administer; that is obvious.
Then hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) is to be congratulated too, also the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) in his few remarks, and the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). I think after all is said and done, it was the few over in that corner that offended on the question of immigration. Some people have the capacity for making considerable noise and getting in the limelight. I feel like exonerating the great bulk of the Progressive party of the charge of disparaging their own country. Why are they doing this, those that are doing it, and how much of it is genuine and how much for political purposes? I am going to make a confession. I can recall when I was in opposition. It was apparently my fate to be born in the county of Lanark where a fellow that was a Liberal was always in opposition, and in the early 90's in the West and the late 80's I can recall when we were all nearly bankrupt and would have been absolutely if it had not been for the Rebellion of '85:	The government of that day, which
was Conservative, would send down some of their members like the present Senator Foster to tell us how to farm. Of course, we got mad and turned around and said, "Here, we have been working at this farming business for years and are getting poorer all the time." In my younger days I used to say just the same kind of foolish things, but surely with the years should come some wisdom, and that is the reason why the leader of the Progressive party has wisdom.
What I want to point out is this. During those days of hardship there was some justification for it, because we had no tradition, we had no history; it was all a question of
what the future of the country was going to be. But we have had forty years' experience now which we can look back upon as an earnest of what can be done in the future. During those bygone years I did take the ground on more than one occasion, especially when a Tory politician from Ottawa came around, that there were enough people already in the West to experiment, and that we should wait before bringing more people in-just exactly what my hon. friend was saying the other day. But there was justification for my saying that then. It was a gamble, an experiment in those days. There were only a few Hudson Bay posts and a few church missions throughout the country to tell what could be done in agriculture. I want to put myself in the same category with the hon. gentleman who was wanting me to define "stability," because I took the same ground, but I think I had some justification. The object was partly political. I am free to make that confession now that thirty years have gone by. It was partly that, and I think it is partly that on their part now. How are they going to get any political advantage out of this? I do not know myself, but the idea as far as I can understand it, and we have seen the same disposition in several of the committees as well as in this House, seems to be to blacken things blacker than your hand. Well, if that is good politics, we cannot throw a lariat around any hon. gentleman and choke him off if he wants to talk that way. This is a free country and we have free speech; there is no closure even, so I suppose we will just have to submit to it. But I understand the feelings of hon. gentlemen. I know the tragedies that have occurred on the prairie. I know homes there that are destitute of the ordinary necessities, let alone the conveniences of life. I know of the hardships because I went through them. I do not wish to refer to myself too much, but I started on the Portage plains as a harvest labourer and I know the business of agriculture, I know its hardships. If a man goes there with youth, courage, determination and health and stays with the job I know he will win out. Where would I go to for a better place to farm?
Mr. MARTELL; Nova Scotia.

Premier Dunning had an experience that I am going to relate. I do not know whether he told it at the Grain Growers' convention at Saskatoon or not, but he said some straight things there. Some person'was croaking about the West There are lots of things that are not very pleasant if you are looking for that black side, and this man was chewing about the black

things of life, when Mr. Dunning said, "I am not a wealthy man, but if you will pick out the place you want to go to I will buy your ticket." Then the gentleman thought he would stay a little while longer. He did not take advantage of the offer. It may have been a bluff, but he did not call it.
Now I wish to refer briefly to the amendment to the budget. That amendment is so remarkably like some features of the budget that it would need the X-ray to distinguish the difference between them. The amendment declares:
And, further, that the best interests of Canada will be served by:-
(a) An immediate and substantial reduction in the tariff, particularly on the necessaries of life and the implements of production.
How many Progressives from the prairies voted for the reductions last year? What encouragement is there for anybody to fight for a thing and have not a single Progressive from the West support it? I think the proper policy when there is a lowering of the tariff is to support what you are getting. The Progressives last year showed the same attitude towards the lowering of the tariff as the Conservatives did. The latter opposed the government's policy because there was too much tariff reduction; the Progressives opposed it because it was too little. Had either proposition been adopted the government would have been defeated. It shows the folly of group parliament. Then this amendment proposes an immediate increase in the British preference to 50 per cent of the general tariff. That is the policy of both the Liberals and the Progressives. The leader of the Progressives, I want to point out, is far too modest in asking for an increase of 50 per cent in the British preference, far too modest. He is asking for something that is already in existence, something which now obtains on many articles although not on every article. I expect that when I read the list of tariff duties which I am about to do my hon. friend will head a deputation to the Finance [DOT] Minister to-morrow telling him that he will have to reduce the British preference in these cases, that it is altogether too high. Let me enumerate some of the tariff items which I got to-day. No doubt.
-of the total list of commodities which this country imports from Great Britain.
I know that. There may be one hundred or two hundred but we have not got round to those yet.
You are a long time getting there.
Will the minister give us the preferential rate on butter?

If we had the
same advantage as our friends the Progressives in the matter of adjusting platforms I do not know in what position we should find ourselves. An interval of twenty-three years elapsed between the conventions held by the Liberals. After such an interval I think it is only right that the platform should
9 p.m. be brushed up. A number of members of the Liberal opposition in parliament took the ground that the Liberal platform of 1919 should be brushed up; in fact was brushed up by a subsequent resolution. I was not there so sometimes it is convenient not to have a past. I know that very strong opinion has been expressed that the platform of the parliamentary members of the party was not the same as the 1919 platform. But two wrongs do not make a right. Surely a platform should not have finality any more than a tariff I have here the platform of the Progressive party. It is quite interesting and I want to comment upon some of the clauses. Here is one extract from it:
By reducing the customs duty on goods imported from Great Britain to one-half the rates charged under the general tariff, and that further gradual uniform reductions be made in the remaining tariff on British imports that will ensure complete free trade between Great Britain and Canada in five years.
That expression "in five years" was dropped off in 1920 and it now might mean five centuries. That was a very convenient expression to knock off from the old Progressive platform. The free trade plank has also been eliminated from the platform. I think the
