Conservatives at least, will consider that as all right. Another plank in the Progressive platform reads thus:
That the Reciprocity Agreement of 1911 which still remains on the United States statute books be accepted by the parliament of Canada.
Did my hon. friend hear the Minister of Finance make his speech? Why repeat part of the budget asking for what they have? They were sorely tried to pad out an amendment when they had asked for a British preference to SO per cent of the general tariff, when it was already 60 per cent, and to ask for reciprocity which they already had in the budget. An oversight must have occurred. Several hon. members probably drafted the amendment; they merged it together, and they had not time to see whether they conflicted with each other or not. This is one of their proposals:
As these tariff reductions may very considerably reduce the national revenue-
They propose this method of raising revenue:
By a direct tax on unimproved land values including all natural resources.
That is their old platform. They have dropped that, and I do not blame them, because it was fallacy. There is nothing about that in the amendment.
What makes the hon. member think we are moving a platform? We are moving an amendment to the budget.
Of course I recognize that. My hon. friend was not present when I pointed out that he had more already than he was asking for.
Just on a few articles. Th:s is not, however, the place to enter into .i debate, but we shall probably have an opportunity at some other time.

That pleases me all right. I was trying to point out, when I was assisted by my hon. friend, that they had the advantage and the wise advantage of being able to change their platform. They are doing that now, and they are omitting a number of things that they previously asked for. Things which they are asking for now, in some important instances they already have.
I think it was stated by the Regina Leader that, in the West, they had one pleasant surprise in the budget, namely the standing offer of reciprocity. It surely was not necessary for any of the oppositions to bring down another budget with the same proposition precisely. That is not an amendment. Moreover, tMr. Motherwell.]
the amendment asks for a British preference to 50 per cent of the general tariff, disregarding the fact that on some twenty-four articles, the preference is from 50 to 60 per cent already. That is quite delightful to me. Whether it is consoling to my hon. friends or not, I do not know. It is the carrying out of both of our platforms, and then some more.
I was wondering, when the minister was quoting from the Regina Leader, if he also noticed what the premier of Saskatchewan thought about the budget.
My hon. friend is three or four laps behind. I have already dealt with that.
I am sorry I had not the pleasure of listening to that'part of the minister's remarks.

They all have the same joke. WTe cannot expect another one. This "blue ruin" talk has developed that kind of thing.
I come now to a very interesting part of the budget with respect to bounties. We are told that it is a protectionist budget. Strange to say, so far as I have been able to determine, the change in every single item in the budget, in which there has been a change, is downwards. How in the world then, do you make out that it is protectionist? Can you make it free trade by putting it up? Can you make it lower by making it higher? If you can, there must be something wrong with this kind of figuring.
Personally I do not see any justification for the amendment on the ground that the budget is protectionist, unless it is as regards the two items upon which bounties have been placed. I wonder upon which of those two items the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) thought he discerned the vicious hydra-head of protection. I do not like protection one bit better than my hon. friend. I was not brought up on that at all.
The hon. member has changed his views.

I should like to know on which of those two articles he thinks he can detect the vicious principle of protection, that interminable protection that you cannot get rid of. A bounty is, admittedly, a species of protection; but it is the least objectionable, and it is terminable rather than interminable.
I do not hear vociferous voices telling me which of these two items constitutes the pro-

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
tectionist feature of the budget. Perhaps hon. members straight opposite will be the authority on protection and can tell me that. I am up against it. I am not an authority myself on protection. That reminds me that there is protection and protection. When I was advocating the establishment of a new industry in Manitoba, the development of the flax industry there, some of the arguments seemed ominously like those which the Tories used to make. I can remember them, but this had the saving virtue that it was going to last only so many years. There is no termination that I can see to the other kind of protection. In my election address at my nomination in Regina, before both urban and rural representatives, I made this statement. I have under my hand what I said. I wrote it down so that I would know:
In a young country like Canada, with so many and varied natural resources, new industries are bound to be springing up from time to time. Any of these that are likely, and indigenous to the country, could, if deemed wise, be directly assisted in a start, by means of loans, guarantees or otherwise, and then gradually withdrawn as the particular enterprise becomes established. Right in this city-
That was in the city of Regina.
-we have two illustrations of such state assistance by the provincial government to the Saskatchewan Cooperative Creameries and the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevators.
State nursing -to exotic industries or industries al-* ready long and well established under a protective tariff is not good ultimately for labour, consumer or anybody else, except the beneficiaries thereof, and is frequently the source from which corruption emanates in our public life.
I am pledged, as a matter of fact my whole provincial experience was along the lines of starting up industries connected with agriculture by some form of state assistance.
Does the minister say that the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company got a bounty?

I did not say that at all. If my hon. friend will sit down, I will tell him what I said. There are other illustrations. I could not be expected to say everything, even in this House. I will refer my hon. friend to an activity that was a straight subsidy, and that was the stockyard at Moose Jaw and the other one at Prince Albert. They were each given a straight subsidy of $25,000. I would not be surprised if my hon. friend has stock in that stockyard. I know I was canvassed for it, and if I had not been hard up, the chances are that I would have had some.
I have a $100 share in it, which I will count as a subsidy to the Moose Jaw stockyard, instead of an investment.

It was after I left
that they gave that.
I am glad to find myself entirely on the side of the amendment in one important respect and that is with regard to the question of the excise. I do not know whether in this weary political world we shall ever get around to that but it is absolutely sound, and it is the only way to take protection out of any tariff. There is no such thing as an exclusively revenue tariff; the question is merely one of degree as between one kind of tariff and another. The tariff may be high enough to be prohibitive, to be protectionist, or it may primarily be just a revenue tariff; but if it is a revenue tariff it is to some extent protectionist. The more general adoption of the excise, we are told, would be most equitable all round and would relieve the poor man accordingly. "I am," the hon. gentleman says, "in theory, if you like, and in practice if I can be, in favour of an excise tariff." If that is so, let him come over and help me get it through. What is one among so many? Let the hon. gentleman come and help me. But that, Mr. Speaker, shows the folly of being divided. If I had not had the experience thirty years ago of having made just exactly the same blunder that my hon. friends are making, I would be on the other side now. But when you make a mistake once what is the sense of making it a second time?
May I ask a question?
Yes, two if you like.
Just one. Does the minister mean to imply that he is the lone wolf howling in the wilderness, and that there is no one on the other side besides himself who holds these views?
I did not say that.
You want us to ijpme and help you.
I did not say anything about wolves or coyotes or anything else.
You cried for help.

I did; and there is no reason why my hon. friend and I should not be on the budget together instead of his submitting the flim-flam proposition that we have here. What is the use of asking for reciprocity? How much more can you get than is offered in the budget?

Speaking seriously, does the minister really want to leave the impression

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
that as a westerner he is satisfied with the present budget?

I am never satisfied with anything in this progressive world; I am always on the lookout for better things. Did the hon. gentleman ever see a Liberal who was satisfied to stay in one place? Now, I was getting around to the subject of twine, and I could not get a reply from my hon. friends from Manitoba as to whether they thought that the budget in this respect was protective. I can recall the time when Manitoba voted eight to two against reciprocity, and I am disposed to think that if they were so vigorous as protectionists at that time they will not object very much to this least objectionable form of protection, particularly when it is likely to establish an industry which we stand in very much need of and for the product of which we should be independent of the outside world. There are two or three primary requisites for which we should not have to depend on foreign countries One of these is coal and another binder twine. I remember that during the war we were at one stage almost with the last ball of twine; and if the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) is in his seat he will no doubt recall that I interceded on his behalf once and got a carload of twine hooked on to an express train that was going to Yorkton, for the purpose of meeting the exigencies of the situation there. We have become, almost overnight, the greatest exporter of wheat in the world. The estimate of the International Institute of Rome shows that we have exceeded the United States by some six or eight million bushels this year in exports of wheat. Yet here we are, the greatest exporter of wheat in the world, bound to depend on foreign nations for 90 per cent of the twine that is used in binding it. We do not want to anticipate any difficulties that may. arise in the future, and probably our relations with our cousins to the south will continue to be cordial. But what about Mexico? A lot of our sisal comes from Mexico and our manilla from the Philippines. Suppose another war should occur, where would we get our binder twine? Why should we depend for our raw materials on places at the ends of the earth, especially for the manufacture of such a commodity as binder twine, or rope, or the various cordage and articles that are made from hemp?	It seems to me that both
this commodity and coal we should be able to produce ourselves; we should be self-sustaining so far as they are concerned. Should we allow any theory, shot 
into us when we were young regarding trade and economic practices, and which may be all right in theory, to prevent us from carrying out such a policy? Such a policy is not contrary to the tenets of the Liberal party. We have had subsidies before and I presume we shall have them again. A high tariff on articles not made in the country is not incompatible with free trade. There are certain things that are not inconsistent with the policies of the Liberal party, and one of those things is the permission of aid to such an industry as this. What would be the situation if we were to take the position that every new industry must either start on its own merits or not start at all? This idea seems to me to be absolutely nonsensical. How can you get capital invested in an industry that is in its experimental stages if it has to face such an old-established industry as, for example, the International Harvester Company? If you have to wait until capital will come in under conditions of that kind you will wait until the crack of doom, because that will never be. So that unless w7e do something to help this industry we shall have to keep on buying 90 per cent of our binder twine outside the shores of Canada. I am not an authority on the copper trade, but I have had an opportunity of visiting some of the hemp factories of Europe, and I know that hemp can be grown and has been grown in Manitoba around Portage la Prairie and the Swan river country. I do not believe there is a man in that province who has not seen it growing; and there are many parts of Saskatchewan in which it can be grown. Under irrigation in Alberta also, particularly around Edmonton, there would be no difficulty in raising this crop. There is therefore an immense industry capable of unlimited development later on which would be able to supply not only our own needs but the oriental trade and the Antipodes as well. Is there any reason why this should not be?
I do not know of any country that can produce this raw material in greater bulk than can the Canadian West. Now, if this is not a protectionist feature of the budget, what is? And if it is a protectionist feature of the minister's proposals, do I understand that hon. gentlemen are opposed to it? Judging from the remarks of the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), that hon. gentleman is heartily in favour of it, as we might have expected. It was not necessary for the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) to put any resolution on the order paper dealing with this matter to indicate where he was. I knew where he would be. I might have sus-

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
pected, from our experience with the Progressives with regard to the Crowsnest pass when they swiped our policy, that any credit that was coming to the government might be encroached upon in the same way by the leader of the Opposition, in the placing of his resolution with regard to hemp on the order paper, the hon. gentleman knowing that we intended to take action in any event. If this swiping business keeps on I think we will soon have to tie on our political clothes with a logging chain. I exonerate the right hon. leader of the Opposition from any such intention. He is a straight protectionist from the word go. He never changes, and we know where he is-if that is any virtue.
If one is a protectionist he is better to be a straight one.
Sure. I am with my right hon. friend. There are certain points of similarity so far as bounties are concerned that I think all three parties could agree to. Then why worry about them? This is one.
Why worry?

Now, Mr. Speaker, I am going to deal with what I think are some discriminations against the West. My hon. friends over there, while they have not, done all they might have done to help themselves, know the shoe pinches in some other respects too. We have known that for many years. But while they are endeavouring to get a certain remedy from the state, that is no reason why they should not come to their own relief through the dozen and one avenues that are available to them, as I have already described. What is the use of sitting back and not adopting modern methods of agriculture? Those are the only methods that can lead to success. Simply waiting for the state to come to your relief in the matter of tariffs or anything else will not get you very far. There is no system of taxation through the customs tariff that will not bear unjustly on the West. That is a statement which T think on reflection you will all agree is correct. At least, such a system of taxation can not be levied so as to bear justly on the West until we have manufactories out there equal to those in the East, and I never expect tr see them. Protection, even the most modest protection you like, cannot be of any essential value to the people of the prairies in the sale of their staple products such as wheat and cattle. Our wheat goes to the markets of the world and sells on its own merits regardless of what the tariff is here. Our steers are going there now, landing at the various ports and
standing on their four feet in competition with every steer from the four quarters of the globe and selling on their merits. How can you protect them? Our butter is coming to that position, too, because we now have an export surplus. I say that any tariff, whether for revenue, protection or otherwise is only a matter of degree, will bear unjustly-will bear unduly perhaps is a better word, because 1 do not think that any of us want to be unjust-on the West. My eastern friends demonstrated that last year when they said: If you can show any of us how the West can be assisted, even by the establishment of what we disprove of-a compulsory wheat board, for instance-we will give it to you so far as is possible to do so through this House. And they did go as far as they could in that direction. I do not think there is any desire on the part of the eastern provinces to be unjust or unfair in continuing a system of tariff taxation that inevitably must be unfair to the West simply because it cannot be otherwise. The alternative is to assume that the millennium is here, that the hundred and ninety-five representatives from the eastern provinces are ready to set their interests aside in favour of the interests of the three prairie provinces. I never expect them to do that. Then how are we going to equalize matters? There are certain causes for the discontent of the West, apart from their mighty bad farming in some instances and equally bad management. They are going into it to-day right to the eyes.
Does the hon. minister claim that in the West there are more bad farmers than good farmers?

I have not been up in my hon. friend's constituency of Battle River so I do not know. But I do know there is a lot of bad farming in the West. When those farmers arrive at that conclusion themselves, it will be the first ray of hope for their betterment. Yes, my hon. friend surely knows there is a lot of bad farming in the West. How could it be otherwise when much of the country was settled by people without farming experience? And yet some of those very people, much to their credit, have made a prenounced success of their farming operations. T know many of them.
Where did I leave off when my hon. friend interrupted me?
It does not make any difference. Star* again.
The cattle were on their feet.

No, the butter.
The Budget-Mr. Motherwell

If my hon. friends will just keep quiet for a little while I shall be able to satisfy them. I have been very patient with them and have enjoyed myself as much as, possibly more than, they have. I want to make an appeal to the entire House with regard to the question of natural resources. It is a time-honoured question in the West. There is never an assembly out there but what that stereotyped resolution is on the order paper All three of the western provinces got a splendid bargain from both the Liberal government and later on from the Conservative government in the form of subsidies in lieu of their natural resources. Those resources now, Mr. Speaker, are actually becoming a liability on the Dominion to administer. Out in the West we are beginning to feel that while we did get a good bargain in that respect, we are sufficiently ambitious and optimistic to think the time has come when we can administer those resources much better ourselves than they can be possibly administered from Ottawa. All the interest that Ottawa has is to administer these resources efficiently so as to get enough revenue to meet the expenditures involved; and that is barely what they are doing. As a matter of fact the revenues are not meeting the expenditures.
Now, why should we not administer our own natural resources? If we are going to be a happy family of nine in the confederation surely we should as nearly as possible be all on an equality. I have pointed out that we cannot be on a footing of equality so long as we have a protective tariff; I do not care how modest it may be it will bear unduly on the West. Then why aggravate that inequality by continuing a condition of affairs which puts three of the nine provinces in an unfair position with regard to their natural resources, particularly when these resources are administered by the Dominion at a loss' How do I know that? I have gone into the Department of the Interior and examined the accounts. I knew the natural resources of the prairie provinces were barely carrying themselves. I am not going to give these figures in detail, I am merely going to show the results of the last 18 years. The total includes immigration and also the Dominion parks, but their inclusion will not affect the total to an appreciable extent. British Columbia is also included in these figures, but the small amount of natural resources there and the difference between the expenditures and the revenue is so little that it will not affect the result either. However, we will knock off several millions on this

account if you like. We find the total expenditure for the four western provinces since 1905-that is when the three prairie provinces were erected-has exceeded the total revenue by approximately $?7,500,000. That is to say, it cost the Dominion that huge total to administer the natural resources of the western country over and above the revenues received. If we knock off "7,500,000 for Dominion parks we find the Dominion is still out to the extent of 820,000,000. That is the liability on the Dominion n respect of the administration of these natural resources.
Now why wait until this liability becomes so much heavier that the provinces will want even greater subsidies in lieu of their administration of these natural resources? That is what is going to happen. Look at the province of Manitoba. It costs in that province
85,000,000 annually to administer the natural resources, and you will not get a million and a half out of it. That is the condition that will soon prevail in Saskatchewan when the instalments for lands that were sold during the boom are all paid in. In Alberta their natural resources are gradually going to bring in more revenue. They are more fortunate than the other two provinces in regard to the permanency of their revenue-producing natural resources, due to their wonderful coal deposits and, possibly, oil deposits. I have discussed this matter not only with my colleagues but with private members, and they are imbued with the idea, that if we get the balance of the natural resources we should give up the subsidy. On the face of it that looks logical, but the fact is that any balance that is left is so small that there is no revenue in it for anybody at this time. Why, not, seeing that this is a liability to the Dominion, pass it over to these three western provinces and make that equality to exist that should prevail among all the members of confederation? Give them the opportunity of converting this liability into an asset to the various provinces. Make the subsidy terminable at some particular time, if you like; the right of that subsidy will then have been purchased by this Dominion forever.
To whom is the hon. member appealing to do this justice?
The whole House.
Would it not be a good idea to bring in a bill?

It takes two to
make a bargain-the provinces and the Dominion. There has never been anything done between the provinces and the Dominion on

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
the question of the resources except by consultation or by conference. Suppose we could get a bill through this House, the provinces might not accept it.
Could the hon. gentleman not succeed in making terms with the government of Saskatchewan that he junt came out of?

The government of Saskatchewan knows when it has a good thing in this bargain and it is not likely to give it up. A year ago last autumn there were suggestions that the natural resources should be given plus three years' subsidy; I believe that offer was made to the three provinces. A flat rate basis of that kind will sooner or later have to be arrived at, but the provinces would not accept the three years' subsidy. They might accept ten; I do not know. It was tentatively talked about. I know that my right hon. friend, as former Minister of the Interior, is familiar with this question and interested in it. It must have some finality-unlike the tariff. I am satisfied that a settlement of it would remove a lot of the grievance on the ground of inequality of treatment through the western provinces not having control of their natural resources. You may say, why should we take over a liability? Well, we believe we can convert them into an asset at some time or other; and they are getting to be more and more of a liability administered where they are. I appeal to every hon. member of this House, those

the oppositions included, to get this involved, knotty, long-standing question solved and put off the order paper.

If the hon. minister will allow me, he knows the terms that he asked for when he was a member of the government of Saskatchewan, and he knows the terms that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) asked for when he was Premier of the province of Alberta. May I ask why this government does not grant these terms? Has he now come to the conclusion that they were unreasonable?
I do not know that any government has ever got as far as to offer the terms that we did at the last conference.
I mean the terms the provinces asked for, that the minister himself asked for when he was in the government of Saskatchewan. Why does he not now grant the terms that he himself asked for?
It was never my fortune to be in the conference. I always had the impression-

The hon. gentleman
asked the terms.

I know, and I take the responsibility for doing so. But nobody knows better than my right hon. friend the ramifications involved in settling that question by an accounting. I cannot conceive of a body getting at that in less than ten years.
I tried to convince the hon. minister of that when I was in power, but I could not convince him.
Better late in getting wise than not at all. I was under the impression that this government was the first government-speaking from recollection-that had made a straight flat rate offer.
Oh, no.
And trimmed it off with all these conditions. I am only speaking from memory, of course.
Oh, no. The hon. minister is about ten years late in that.

I am glad my right hon. friend did think up something that was right during his regime. I am appealing to my right hon. friend's good nature. I see that he is in good humour, and I do not want to put him otherwise.

Does my hon. friend not think that we were pretty nearly right on the tariff too?
Mr. MOTHERW-ELL. No. Some of it you cannot get away from, I admit, but you were not right, just the same.
Now, as to these natural resources, we are going to get further in wrong, we are going to get a greater liability. The instalments on the Saskatchewan land will all be due next year; the same applies to Alberta. After that the receipts will gradually grow less and the deficit will grow greater. We will have one more deficit added to that of the Merchant Marine, one more added to that of the National Railways-which, by the way, I hope will soon disappear altogether. There is no sense in letting one deficit disappear and having another bob up on the horizon like this one, but that is what will happen. I appeal to hon. members of this House, all of them, to consider the advisability of handing these re-

The Budget-Mr. Sexsmith

sources over on some conditions associated with a terminable period of years after which the payment of subsidies would stop. Naturally the number of years would be smaller in the case of Alberta than in the case of the other two provinces. I am not going to suggest how many years should be stipulated, but in my opinion that is the proper basis on which to arrive at an agreement.
I apologize for taking up so much time, but I think the responsibility is equally divided over the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. SEXSMITH (Lennox and Addington) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am persuaded that my contribution to this verbal deluge will not, perhaps, be of very great value. Still, on account of the importance of the subject before the House I feel it incumbent upon me to express some of my opinions in connection with this budget.
I admit that the task of discharging the duties of a finance minister is a tremendous one, involving perhaps more labour and care and ability than many of us have a true conception of. Therefore I find mingled in my suggestions this evening feelings of sympathy and respect for our worthy Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding). Perhaps in my remarks tonight I may deviate somewhat from the general line of discussion that has been followed. I desire not to be specific but to talk along lines of general principles.
Canada has a debt of approximately two and a half billion dollars. If we consider this debt in comparison with her undeveloped abilities or her resourceful wealth we have grounds for optimism; but if we consider this debt in comparison with her volume of business and her population this problem is a bit more serious. Yet I take it, Mr. Speaker, that every statesman, every representative should have a determination and express that determination that this debt can and must be paid. Indeed every citizen should feel that Canada is his country and that the defeat or success of Canada means his personal defeat or success, that the distinguishment of the country means his distinguishment. A national debt means a depreciation in the value of individual possession. Therefore, every one should feel that it is his imperative duty to endeavour to pay this debt of the country. In order to make this privilege proportionately possible governments have as far back as we can remember resorted to taxation.
In raising the revenue there are certain fundamental principles to be observed. Governments try if possible to bring down a

balance budget, or to go one better and bring in a surplus, but when large war debts accrue and post-war conditions obtain I apprehend, Mr. Speaker, that to bring down taxation proposals that would produce a surplus in any one fiscal year might not be the wisest policy to followi It might create demands that would encourage and lower the morale of the people and retard national progress. We, however, both governments and citizens, should try to decrease the deficit. In the report brought down by the Finance Minister fof the fiscal year 1922-1923 we were told that the revenue estimated on the then existing method of taxation amounted to something like $332,000,000 and that the expenditure was $460,000,000 odd. This convinced, or should have convinced, the people of Canada of the necessity of accepting the burden of additional taxation, but I am free to state that no hon. gentleman here decided within his own mind that we would have a balanced budget, that there would not be an increase in the deficit. In talking to many people in my riding I estimated that there would be a deficit of perhaps twenty or thirty million dollars. I regret, however, to learn that that deficit amounts to about forty-five million dollars. Now we are facing a condition. The business of Canada will not permit an increase in taxation. Neither would it be wisdom to decrease our revenue from taxation. Then whence is relief to come?
I wish by way of constructive suggestion to refer to two well-tried principles that are fundamental in this connection; First, an increase in national business, and secondly economic retrenchment in financial expenditure. It is necessary for Canada to have more people. You cannot have a greater business unless you have more people. Our population is about nine million; the population of the United States is about one hundred and twenty million. I would therefore suggest that the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures should co-operate in a vigorous policy of an effective kind to induce immigrants to come into our country. No matter what their vocation in life, so long as they are not abnormalities, speaking in the broad sense of the word, let them come. We are not importing machines; we are importing men and women, men who are eager and willing to start at the bottom of the ladder. Men who start at the bottom of the ladder generally look up, but the man who starts at the top generally looks down. If we get enough people who will appreciate the

The Budget-^-Mr. Sexsmith
great privileges that the Dominion of Canada has for them, and will take hold of these privileges, that will be a great help in increasing our business. Along with that I would suggest that the government of Canada try in every possible way to develop our natural resources. Canada is rich in minerals, and I was pleased to hear the Finance Minister speak of the efforts put forward for the mining of copper. I hope that there will be efforts put forward for the mining of coal, for I believe that we have coal mines in Canada capable of supplying our people with all their fuel requirements. It is true that in its early development any mine or any works might not pay, but if we persist the time will come when the output will be prolific enough that it will pay. The development of the natural resources and more people in this country mean more business.
Let me now take up my second thought, economic retrenchment. It is true that in the development of a country the spirit of miserliness must be forgotten. We must carry on necessary public works, but it does seem to me sometimes and to others who have spoken to me that parliaments that handle money by the millions of dollars seem to forget the value of the hundred dollars. Of course, we know that all departments try in every possible way, or at least they ought to, to curtail unnecessary expenditure, but I sometimes think that the members do not try very hard to do this. They come here with requests from the different provinces and from the people of their riding for all manner of new public works, post offices, dry docks and so forth.
What about the Hudson Bay railway?

I think it is only right that members should consider the financial condition of the country and not encourage those who ask them to try and further such works. It would be a help to the men who have the responsibility of carrying on these works.
Let me mention a few things that, perhaps, may not be very popular. Aside from the expenditures on public works, economies might be effected in other directions which would save, I think, millions of dollars to the treasury. With all due respect to the late government, as well as to the present government, the administration of the country's affairs is far too expensive and has been for some years. I am well aware that my suggestionsfefor retrenchment may be unacceptable. Tft'ey certainly will not be very popular in the city of Ottawa. However, I want to make a few remarks as to the cost of government here and if I am wrong in any respect I am quite ready to be corrected. First of all, there must be a retrenchment in expenditures in connection with the Civil Service. I voted for an investigation into the salaries, classification and numbers of the staff of the Civil Service. It seems to me that the investigation which is being conducted into these matters ought to result in a very substantial saving. Salaries are disproportionately high. They have been increased from time to time because it was the custom so to do. In that respect we have been following a practice which obtains in other countries, with the result that the stipends are in very many cases too high.
Then I would restrict, in great measure, the expenditure on superannuation and retiring allowances. Why should men who have been receiving large salaries for the greater part of their lives receive a retiring allowance when quitting the service when hundreds of thousands of people who are following vocations that are essential from the standpoint of the national well-being and who are in every way good and commendable citizens get no such allowance when the time comes for them to quit work. This question has been impressed upon the public mind by the very large amounts granted to officials of the government railways on retirement. The electors are asking why, for example, a railway president who has been receiving a salary of from $35,000 to $50,000 should be retired on an allowance of $35,000. If the expenditures of the public departments are carefully studied it will be found that there are many directions in which retrenchment is possible thus, possibly, causing a saving which could be devoted to the reduction of our national debt.
I want to speak now for a moment or two on the question of taxation. As fair minded citizens we cannot rebel against just and equitable taxation, but we can protest against extravagance and we, as a parliament, can show the lead to the rest of the country by practising economy ourselves. To my mind when budget proposals are brought down the effort should be to relieve the burden of taxation where it bears heaviest upon the great mass of what I might term unprivileged people, and to impose such taxation as is necessary in the interests of the revenue upon those best able to bear it. At the same time I do not believe in the doctrine of equality which we often hear preached: I think that is something which ought to be discouraged as undemocratic. On the other hand, men who are in
The Budget-Mr. Sexsmith

responsible positions should do their utmost to discourage that spirit of selfishness and graft, too often present in the human character, and which in the past has resulted in oppression, the oppression of the financially weak by the financially strong. I know, Mr. Speaker, that it is exceedingly difficult to arrange equitable methods of taxation. There are
10 p.m. some methods that commend themselves to all of us; there are other methods that we do not approve of. It seems to me, for example, that there could be no fairer tax than the income tax. Nevertheless we find people who have never paid a cent of income tax in their lives raising the greatest outcry in regard to it. I also believe that a business tax is fair. If a man is conducting a good business he certainly can afford to pay a tax of some kind. Then there is a consumer's tax. If it is absolutely such as represented and can be made workable I cannot see that there is anything so particularly wrong about it, provided due regard be paid to the principle of which I have spoken. I had intended saying something about the sales tax because in calling upon different business concerns in my own riding complaint was made that it was unworkable. I understand, however, that the Minister of Finance, having had various deputations wait upon him has made the necessary changes so that the same ground for criticism no longer exists. There are some methods of taxation of which I certainly do not approve. The tax, whether direct or indirect in its nature, which builds up one industry at the expense of another is unfair. It is based on special privilege which is unjust and will result in bringing about an unbalanced economic condition.
In 1878 or 1879, Sir John A. Macdonald introduced his National Policy, a policy to build up cities. I remember hearing a speech delivered by him in our county town, to the effect that if you build up your towns, your cities, you build up home markets, and thereby you build up your country. All this, however, had to be done at the expense of the rural districts. Nobody ever built up a city from above, nor from below. This, to my mind, has obtained too long in the interest of the cities' wealth and the cities' privileges, and it has resulted in the neglect of rural interests. People are expecting a revision of this policy. Not only have I heard men who believe in the Liberal platform or in the Progressive platform, but I have talked during the last year to men who professed to be Conservatives, and they say emphatically that there must be a downward revision of this protective feature.

Leaving for a moment this campaign football, the tariff, let me say that there are other questions of momentous concern for men who are in responsible positions as ministers of the Crown or even as representatives of the people. There are forceful organizations which are national octopuses, and they are chaining the hands of governments and parliaments. In North America, governments are strangled; they are helpless. The forceful feature, for instance, in the labour unions- and I say this with all respect to labour-has become reactionary. There was a time when labour was not recognized as it should be. I know that because for several years when I was younger I worked as a mechanic; I have associated with such men and I know whereof I speak. But silently and subtly, this union has been working until the plumb line has gone the other way. Strikes are unprofitable from the fact that they throw men into idleness for a certain length of time during the season, and they keep up the high cost of living the whole season around. Vigorous efforts should be made to try, by commission work and in every other way, to see if there cannot be some conciliation between labourers and their employers. During the height of the coal strike in the United States, President Harding is reported as saying that the United States government would take over the mines and they would see that the people were supplied with the necessary fuel. Immediately after that he received word that he had better go slowly and be considerate, or transportation would be stopped. This is a serious condition. It is a more important matter to occupy the minds of men in responsible positions than for them to play party politics.
There are other unions which are fixing, maintaining and controlling prices, and it is a problem to know how to manage them. Retailers report that in many lines of merchandise their price is fixed from above, and that price is maintained by controlling the outlet. Would it be justifiable, if it were possible, for those engaged in agricultural pursuits to form unions, combines, and monopolies, and to fix the price of the foodstuffs of the world? Certainly that would not be right. That is the very feature of protection or monopolies in any respect that we as Progressives stand against. I am sure that organizations or industries that are financially strong enough to form combines of that nature do not need protection. It will be to the eternal honour of some government to at some time make this decision and, in spite of any influences whatever, act upon it.

The trouble with the agricultural industry to-day is, plainly speaking, that the prices of all the supplies that the man who is engaged in agricultural pursuits requires, are so governed by combines that he has nothing to say. If he cannot afford to buy those supplies, there is no use in saying so; the prices are fixed, and it will be observed that when prices can be controlled, they are not fixed, maintained and controlled without a commensurate profit being given. On the other hand, if an agriculturist has anything to sell, there appears an army of respectable people, of course, whom you could not coax or persuade in any way to go out on a farm. They cannot ask too much because the consumer cannot buy the article, so they have to go the other way and force the price down on the agriculturist until it is almost impossible to coax or persuade young men to continue in agricultural pursuits. We hope that the very effective work of the different parliamentary committees, together with the Combines Act, will tend to relieve conditions. As regards the budget, I must confess that I am very much disappointed. We were told some things last year that we thought justified us in supporting the minister's budget at that time. be a reduction in the tariff. That is the part I object to. The amendment is more elaborate than I should like, but there are principles in it which I feel will compel me to give it my support.

I do not know which member of the Liberal ministry is responsible for the policy of this budget, but he might be likened to the good old John Silver, that man of attractive yet questionable genius. T think that if we could put a wooden leg on the Minister of Agriculture himself he would fill the character very well. Whoever else on this side of the House has failed to appreciate the present budget, its policy, its delicate con-

cessions to the people of Canada, I shall try in the few minutes at my disposal to do it what justice I can.
During the war, and under the stress of the conditions that prevailed then, very many experiments were tried in federal taxation. These included the sales tax, the customs war tax, the income tax, the business tax and the luxury tax, the two latter of blessed memory. Some of these were rough and ready means of raising money in a time of stress and were justifiable solely from that standpoint. But we are no longer at war and it might reasonably have been expected that before this some sincere effort would have been made to place our taxation on a more equitable basis. Instead of that, last year the Minister of Finance chose to perpetuate these crude methods and not only to perpetuate them but to make them bear more onerously upon those elements of the community that always find it difficult to bear any extra burdens of any kind. I think we may be grateful that the income tax is still with us. It is probably the tax that is most easily adapted to the requirements of equity and the economists tell us that it is the only tax that will stay where it is placed. It is a tax that exacts money where it is expected that money can be got. I do not say that our present income tax law comes anywhere near to that ideal. I am sure it does not; it is clumsily and inequitably graduated. The well-to-do people of Canada are not taking a fair share of the burden of Canada's taxation.
We have heard many expressions of appreciation of England during this session. In that wonderful little island the principle of noblesse oblige is practical politics, and the well-to-do person is expected to pay a fair share of the country's expenses. For instance, a man in receipt of an income of $10,000 over there pays in income tax an amount equal to about 18 per cent of his income. In Canada a man in receipt of a similar income would pay about 9 per cent. The well-to-do person, the person who has the good things of life, is getting off very easy in this country at the present time.
There is another defect in our income tax law that might very well be remedied, namely, the failure to discriminate against unearned income-income which comes without any effort or enterprise on the part of the recipient. At the present time there is about a billion and a half dollars in the hands of well-to-do Canadians that did not exist until the war had been in progress for two or three years. That is to say, an income of over $50,000,000' a year was diverted by war into the pockets of
[Mr. BirdJ
certain people. According to all the rules of equity such income ought to bear an extra share of the expenses of government, especially when more than half of our national expend-tiuro is for purposes arising out of the war. In a word, this is the income of people who do not sow, neither do they spin.
There is another form of tax neglected by our federal government, no matter which party is in power and no matter whether we are at war or at peace; I refer to an inheritance tax. This is a form of property upon which the state has had an unchallenged claim from time immemorial. There never was a time in the memory of man when the state did not have a claim upon both real and personal estate at the moment it passed from one generation to another. A short while ago I was reading that even the contemporaries of the late lamented King Tutankhamen of Egypt paid inheritance duties, and I rather think that is the best explanation yet of that monarch trying to carry so much property with him-he was evidently dodging the inheritance tax. We know that the Roman statesman of old, who laid the foundations of much of our present system of statecraft, thought the most appropriate end that could come to an affluent career was some form of compulsory bequest to the state, and they saw to it that such careers were so fittingly closed. Let us look at little England again- a never-failing source of sound precedent, I notice, to certain hon. members. Those lovers of the constitution who are so well sprinkled over the benches of this Chamber when any uncomfortable constitutional question arises always look to England for their precedents. Well now, as soon as England emerged from its political tutelage, at the time of the Revolution her statesmen imposed a tax of (bis kind, and it has been kept in force in more or less the same form ever since.
Now, it seems to me that such an inheritance tax approaches as nearly as a tax possibly can to the principle of painless extraction. It hurts nobody. That it is a perfectly just claim established by time, reason and sound democracy, cannot be denied. Therefore it seems rather odd that our federal government should so long have overlooked this source of revenue. I would go as far as to say that all our sister dominions have adopted such a tax, for the reason that in most of their legislatures there is a greater carefulness for the interests of the common people than has been displayed in this House for a good many years. Indeed, when it comes to the principle of equity in taxation Canada is the laggard of the British Empire.

The Budget-Mr. Bird
The principle of discrimination to which I have already referred was recognized during the war to some extent in the business profits tax. The history of the imposition of that tax is very significant as illustrating the spirit that has prevailed in this House, irrespective of party, towards equity in taxation. There was a tax that, while it contributed very justly to the cost of the war yet was inaugurated very timidly, very tentatively, very apologetically, and it was provided with a kind of automatic stop lest, I suppose, some future finance minister-possibly a Progressive-might forget to stop it. That is one of the pieces of legislation that is not altogether rare in our history whereby a law comes to a silent unseen termination and nobody is the wiser. And so the business profits tax was allowed to go out of existence. It was a just tax, an equitable tax, a tax which if in existence to-day would to a great extent relieve the consuming people, the common people of Canada.
That leads me to a brief discussion of the sales tax and its failure to discriminate against luxuries. The luxury tax was inaugurated on May 19,	1920, and after a short,
unwelcome existence it went out of this world of fiscal sorrows on	the
20th of December of the same year. The circumstances surrounding its death were very significant-just as significant as the circumstances surrounding the death of the business profits tax. The former Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) said some very touching things at the graveside. He said in effect: "It has fulfilled its purpose; it has checked extravagance and lowered the cost of living in this country." Above everything else- he did not actually say this, but it must have been in his mind-it made it easier for the people to swallow the sales tax. There is no doubt that that was the hidden motive behind the luxury tax. It was imposed at the same time as the sales tax. When this tax was dropped the opposition of that day, constituting the present party in power, were silent; they were suspiciously acquiescent; they consented to its death. I think I am right in imputing that attitude to them, because the present Minister of Finance has not, so far as I know, as much as mentioned luxury taxes during the last two years. It is true that one lone voice was raised against the elimination of this tax, that of a gentleman who until recently sat in the ministerial seat but is now translated to a better position, without the responsibility of office. The protest made by that gentleman was remarkable because of its picturesqueness, its biblical imagery. He said: "The Minister
of Finance is pandering to the millionaire. He has stood by and allowed the Queen of Sheba to mince past in her furs and diamonds and all her gay apparel, while he has stood by, with a cudgel for the poor workingman." That came from the Opposition benches when the luxury tax was dropped. I have wondered how that fervent advocate of the poor man felt last year when the hon. minister allowed not only the Queen of Sheba to go by, but also King Solomon in all his glory, while the minister lay in ambush, with a club twice as big this time, for the poor workingman. These are the kind of discussions we get in this House; things are allowed to pass quietly; they are never known to the public at large. Taxes are born and taxes die, both parties consenting thereto. We have this silent, invisible pact whereby the masses of the people always get the heavy end of the burden, and the well-to-do people get things easy.
I want to say a word further in regard to the principle of indirectness as it predominates in the taxation of this country. Canadian governments, it does not matter whether Liberal or Conservative, believe in taxing the consumer-and "the consumer" means that entity which we sometimes refer to as the common people, the great mass of the people who are not very well able to bear taxes upon the necessities of life. This House, irrespective of party, believes in taxing the consumer, making the consumer pay for the war, making the consumer pay for the cost of government. The figures for 1922 show that the consumers of this country paid in that year 67 per cent of the money raised in taxes to carry on the affairs of the country. I think I am safe in saying that in no other country in the English-speaking world do any such figures apply. When we come to apportioning taxation, irrespective of what government is in power, the poor man gets it every time. The hon. member	for Fort	William (Mr. Manion)
this	afternoon suggested that Great
Britain laid very heavy taxation upon the necessities of life; that in spite of the fact that it was a free trade country, Great Britain was making things very burdensome for the poor people. Now, I want to say that in Great Britain the principle of laying the burden where it can most easily be borne is carried out to the fullest extent. There not more than 30 per cent of the cost of running the country is laid at the door of the consumer. I could go a great deal further than that, because I am just referring to what is collected under customs and excise. I think the hon. member for Fort William referred to these as neces-

sities of life, but I would point out that customs and excise taxation in England correspond to our excise taxes here. I want to know how many necessities of life are included in our excise taxes? Nobody but a Scotchman would call spirits a necessity of life, and that is about all that is contained in the British customs and excise-except' sugar, of course, and sugar is taxed fairly heavily. The same applies to tea, matches, and, to some extent dried fruit. Outside of these things there is nothing that can at all be called a necessity of life. I do not think that more than 5 per cent of the total British revenue is raised upon the necessities of life. I would not be so unfair as to say that 67 per cent of our income is raised from the necessities of life, but the great bulk of our revenue comes from the consumer, is laid upon what he purchases and what he uses. That is a serious thing for Canada, a country that is finding great difficulty in maintaining its population. The people are just slipping through our fingers all the time. Some time ago there were a good many allusions to this subject and I do not want to cover the ground again, but .since the Minister of Agriculture has been handing out congratulations I think I will follow his example and hand out a few more. The gratitude of this House-I do not suppose it will be expressed in a formal manner-is coming to those upon this side who attempt to bring the House face to face with the facts. It takes a courageous man to tell the truth sometimes, and that is exemplified from what has followed in this House from action along those lines. I have been pleased to note that since some Progressives made it the fashion to tell the truth, others have followed suit; it is not so hard to tell the truth once somebody has broken the ice. Not long ago the attention of the House was drawn to a front page article in a responsible and influential western journal which stated that last winter 6,000 families had gone from its own city to the United States. I notice that the Minister of Agriculture, when he referred to that journal, did not make the reference with perfect equanimity; he is not on very good terms with it just at this time. The reason is thaf the minister feels that public opinion in the West is going one way and he is left alone to go the other way. I am reminded of the story of the little boy who went with his mother to see his big brother's regiment off to the war. They saw the regiment march down the street, and the little fellow said "Mother, look! They are all out of step but our John." Now it seems that the Minister of Agriculture does 
not like it because that great organ of public opinion in the West is going in the opposite direction to him. But we are very glad that it is. We are very glad to think that one of the most powerful organs of western opinion is coming around to the opinion as expressed in this House a few weeks ago. This is not only a western matter. The other day on the front page of a very important American daily I saw an article in which the present leader of the Opposition was represented as saying that thousands of people were leaving Canada every day because of the high cost of living. Now when I read that statement and saw that it was not associated with the name of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) I had a grand and glorious feeling. After all it is not the Progressives alone that are telling the truth. The Progressives having made it easy to tell the truth the others are beginning. It is going around this way to my right and it may be that it will get across to the other side.
I do not think I can let that go quite unchallenged. I did not make a statement so strong as that. I do not know where the hon. member read it. I went to the limit of the truth but no further.

The hon. member will have to settle his accounts with the New York Tribune. He did say incidentally of course, that the high cost of living was due to the management of our friends across the way, but I thought it not advisable to say that. In that article there was another thing with which the right hon. leader of the Opposition had nothing whatever to do. This article on its own account, I believe, said that on a certain day in Montreal there were four hundred skilled Canadian workmen who applied to the United States consul for entry into the United States. That was in Montreal, not Winnipeg, I may add to these a little news item that I collected from a local paper in my own district at home which read like this: We are sorry to see so many of our Swedish neighbours leaving us; four families left last week for the United States. Mr. Speaker, that is the kind of immigrant that is held up to us as being most capable of adapting himself to conditions as they are in Canada. So from city, town and hamlet they go in thousands and tens of thousands. Then there comes along a certain type of patriot and says: Do not mention it; hush it up; breathes there a man with soul so dead that he will draw the world's [DOT] attention to a thing like that? An open vein spouting out the rich, red life of Canada, and these lachrymose

patriots say: Cover it up; bring a funnel and pour in more; bring a force pump and pump it in; bring Mr. Coue and let us cure it by auto-suggestion; let us woo the immigrant in, and check immigrants from going out; let us cure these things by simply denying them. Now some people call that patriotism, but we on this side of the House call it stark foolishness.
Now there is another side to this inequitable taxation story besides the national one.
I do not see how you are going to attract people from countries where they leave the poor alone, into a country where they make a practice of giving them the heavy end. Apart from that, this is a social question. This iniquitous system of taxation that has prevailed in this country before and during the war and is carried on now succeeds in accentuating unjust conditions that already existed apart from it. I am referring more particularly to the farming community in this country, because I am more particularly associated with them. Some hon. members in dealing with this question of farming conditions have pointed to other countries and said: Look at the farmers in other countries, you Canadians. See how they are getting on. If you only take stock of farming in England and the United States and other places you will be satisfied to stay in Canada. Mr. Speaker, that is poor comfort. It is the kind of comfort that Job got. It means this: You are trying to comfort the Canadian farmer by showing him how widespread his trouble is. I think he could endure it if he thought it was only local, but when he is told it is a world-wide condition, that farmers are getting it in the neck throughout the universe, that is pretty hard on the spirit of the farmer.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, the agricultural industry throughout the world for the past few generations has been gradually pushed into the background by growing industrialism. The farmers throughout the world have wakened up at last to find they are living in a world that has been moulded to suit the ideals and aims of urban life. Educational, social, fiscal, financial, in transportation, in almost every important economic item that you can mention, our modern life has been switched away from the fanner, and it does not matter what country you lay your finger on you will find the same thing. This trying to compare British farmers with Canadian farmers does not amount to-that! The Canadian farmer and the British farmer are suffering from the same thing-the neglect of governments that did not understand them
and did not want to understand them, that bid for their votes at election time but when it came down to their economic difficulties they did not know and did not want to know.
I say this is true whether of the British farmer or of the Canadian farmer, and the fact that the British farmer wants protection and the Canadian farmer free trade makes my point all the more clear if you will only think about it. Free trade and protection does not matter that much! It is the negligence, the callousness of governments that have not tried to understand the principles that govern rural life and the industry of the farmer. Yes, the world has been aroused, "a green international" has come into being and the farmers throughout the world feel that they are standing on common ground. This has resulted in what? It has resulted in the birth of certain political forces that have shaken the old political parties to their foundations-in England the National Farmers' Union, a non-political body but exercising tremendous political influence, in the United States the Farmers' Bloc, an inter-party body that absolutely dominates the parties in the United States, in Canada a direct political movement that may not dominate the old parties but it has them pretty well worried, and it will have them more worried yet, mark my words! In Canada this movement has taken its most logical course because the Canadian farmer stands in this world as being the man who relatively is the worst off. I say relatively advisedly, because the Canadian farmer has no business to be as badly off in a rich country like ours as farmers in other parts of the world. Relatively speaking conditions have pressed most hardly upon the Canadian farmer, and it has resulted in a party so sane in its demands, so democratic and broad in its constitution-
